transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-13
Start: 09:30 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Jamal Owens (Rivermark Head of ML), Priya Shah (Platform Eng), Mark Li (Security), Aisha Gomez (PM)

Summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on latency tuning. Reviewed last week's microbenchmarks (TTFT and steady-state), discussed streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs, sequence length distribution, and kernel selection. Agreed on a kernel sweep (A100/H100 variants) and to share production seq-len histograms to refine batching/cache config. Security docs and pilot pricing to be shared next.

Topics:
- TTFT (time to first token) regressions observed in streaming under small batch workloads
- Effect of sequence length variance on batching and KV cache warm starts
- Kernel selection (cuDNN fused attention vs Triton custom kernels) and quantization tradeoffs
- Dedicated burst policy and expected cost/latency SLOs

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: okay everyone good morning uh thanks for hopping on, let's kick off. quick roll call?
[00:10] Jamal: yep jamal here, priya and mark and aisha on my side.
[00:15] Priya: hi all, priya here.
[00:18] Ethan: ethan cole from redwood se, good to see folks.
[00:22] Sofia: great, so agenda - quick recap of last week's numbers, deep dive on the TTFT spikes you saw, then plan for kernel sweep and data gathering. sound right to you jamal?
[00:31] Jamal: yeah sounds good. we had two things we wanted to confirm - one, those first-token delays we saw in streaming mode at low qps, and two, whether dedicated nodes would help without blowing up cost.
[00:42] Ethan: okay i'll summarize the microbenchmarks we ran. last night we ran the 8k and 2k context models on both H100 and A100. overall steady-state throughput looked good, but TTFT - time to first token - increased in streaming when batch size was one and the request hit an uncached prefix. we saw p50 TTFT around 80ms but p95 jumped to ~420ms on some runs.
[01:06] Priya: just to clarify, those numbers are on your hosted infra tests or on our dedicated pilot?
[01:11] Ethan: hosted infra, using the pilot config you gave (2x H100 equivalent). we tried both cuDNN fused kernels and our triton path; the big TTFT variance correlated with kernel cold starts and kv cache warm-up.
[01:23] Jamal: kv cache? do you mean KV cache warmup, like when the model hasn't seen a prefix so attention kvs aren't populated?
[01:28] Ethan: yeah sorry, kv cache warm-up - sometimes the cache needs a couple of steps to fill and the streaming pipeline waits, which spikes the first token.
[01:33] Mark: is that a memory allocation thing or a kernel compilation thing? security-wise we need predictable tail latencies.
[01:39] Ethan: good question. it's a mix. on H100 we saw a small compilation penalty for the custom triton kernels on first invocation - that was transient. on A100 the triton kernels were slightly slower but had less jitter. also memory allocator behavior can add latency if fragments cause reallocation - that manifests in some runs.
[01:55] Priya: interesting. our workload has a heavy long-tail of sequences - most requests are short 64-128 tokens but ~7% hit 2k+. does that match what you tested?
[02:05] Ethan: we tested both fixed 128 and a mixed distribution sampled from your sample prompts, but we don't yet have your production histogram. that matters because batching strategies and prefix caching rely on the seq-len distribution.
[02:16] Jamal: we'll extract and share that today - priya can take that?
[02:20] Priya: yeah i'll export 30 days of request lengths and send as CSV.
[02:24] Sofia: perfect, that will let us tune batching parameters and decide if we should do per-route kernel pinning.
[02:30] Aisha: quick question on streaming vs non-streaming - do you recommend streaming for low-latency first-byte, or is non-streaming better because it avoids kernel overhead?
[02:38] Ethan: generally streaming helps perceived latency by sending tokens as they're generated, but TTFT can suffer if the pipeline stalls on first token due to JIT/compilation or cache misses. non-streaming (return once) can sometimes be faster for small completions because it avoids context switches, but you lose token-level interactivity. it's a tradeoff.
[02:55] Jamal: for our use case - real-time risk scoring - first token matters for user experience, so we care about p95 TTFT < 150ms ideally.
[03:05] Ethan: understood. with a few levers we can get there: pre-warming kernels, enabling persistent execution contexts (hot-cache), and small-batch reserved capacity. also prefix-level caching for repeated prompts helps a lot.
[03:17] Priya: how big is the pre-warm cost? like if we warm 100 contexts across nodes, does that double memory or is it negligible?
[03:24] Ethan: it increases reserved memory but isn't linear. persistent contexts hold KV allocations; on a 40GB GPU it's noticeable but manageable. we'll quantify in the kernel sweep.
[03:31] Mark: security question - persistent contexts keep some state in GPU memory, is that encrypted or accessible? we need to know retention, wipe guarantees.
[03:37] Ethan: we surface context lifecycle controls in Redwood Private/Dedicated. contexts are ephemeral and we zero memory on teardown; for Private you can enforce host-level encryption and key management. i'll include the memory lifecycle docs in the packet.
[03:50] Sofia: noted - mark, we'll send the SOC2 stuff and a doc on KMS + HSM integration.
[03:56] Mark: thanks.
[03:58] Ethan: back to kernels - we recommend testing both cuDNN fused attention and our Triton custom kernels; fused kernels are great for throughput but sometimes have higher jitter for short sequences. triton is more consistent at small batch sizes. quantization (int8) can cut latency but may affect quality; we did a quick int8 pass and saw modest latency gains but small quality drift on specific prompts.
[04:20] Jamal: what's your recommended path during the POC? we don't want quality regressions.
[04:24] Ethan: start with fp16 cuDNN for steady-state throughput, run Triton for low-batch streaming paths, and use selective int8 on non-critical routes. we'll run a kernel sweep and provide TTFT/p95/p99 numbers across variants.
[04:38] Priya: and batching - should we batch aggressively or keep batch sizes small? our traffic is bursty with lots of single-user requests.
[04:45] Ethan: dynamic batching helps if you can tolerate slightly higher tail for individual requests. but for risk scoring where per-user latency matters, a small max batch (2-4) with shorter wait time (5-10ms) plus hot-cache reduces cost without blowing up TTFT. we'll propose specific parameters after seeing your seq-len histogram.
[04:59] Aisha: any notes on orchestration - if we move to Dedicated, can we pin a model version per route? we need deterministic behavior for audits.
[05:06] Sofia: yes - Redwood Dedicated lets you pin model versions and kernel profiles per route; rollouts support canary and automatic fallbacks. that's part of the Dedicated config we're sizing.
[05:15] Jamal: cost - the Dedicated burst policy you mentioned, how does that work?
[05:19] Sofia: it's basically reserved baseline capacity for steady usage and burst credits for spikes. you pay for baseline reserved, bursts are metered but at a discounted rate versus on-demand. we'll include an example pricing sheet.
[05:29] Priya: ok good. one more technical: those TTFT spikes - any quick mitigations we can apply immediately?
[05:35] Ethan: yes - immediate steps: 1) enable kernel pre-warm for production routes, 2) reduce streaming pipeline headroom to avoid wait-for-kv behavior (tweak the first-token dispatch), 3) pin triton kernels for low-batch routes. i can push a config change to your pilot cluster tonight if you want.
[05:50] Jamal: please do that, ethan. we'll watch telemetry.
[05:53] Ethan: great - i'll schedule that for tonight; i'll also attach the microbenchmark scripts so priya can reproduce locally.
[05:59] Priya: awesome.
[06:02] Mark: security again - memory wipe and audit logs need to be in the plan before production.
[06:07] Sofia: we'll include audit log retention and the KMS integration guide with the SOC2 redacted reports.
[06:12] Aisha: any blockers on our side?
[06:15] Jamal: just the seq-len histogram and the approval for kernel pre-warm in dev tonight - both should be fine.
[06:22] Sofia: recap of next steps for this week - ethan runs kernel sweep and pushes pre-warm config, priya sends seq-len csv, sofia sends pricing and security docs. we reconvene same time next week?
[06:33] Jamal: yep next tuesday works.
[06:35] Priya: one more small ask - can you include sample logs showing KV cache hit rates so we understand cold/warm behavior?
[06:41] Ethan: yes i'll add cache hit/miss metrics and the sample logs.
[06:44] Sofia: perfect. thanks everyone - we'll follow up over email with links to the benchmark results and docs.
[06:51] [00:00:00] Call ended

Notes on transcription: minor speaker attribution errors may be present; a few acronyms mis-transcribed (e.g., kv cache shown as "K-V cash" in auto transcript). Links shared: [microbench scripts] (link), [pilot pricing sheet] (link), [SOC2 redacted] (link).
